title: Following the Money
briefing: Optional specialism: fraud risk. After recent cases, the Audit Committee asks for a fraud risk assessment across Valtren.
Map where fraud could happen and which controls would stop it.

evidence.title: Key processes
evidence.body: Supplier payments (2,400 a month), expenses, fuel cards, payroll, customer credit notes.

evidence.title: Existing controls
evidence.body: Payment approval by budget holder; no check of supplier bank-detail changes; fuel cards without vehicle matching; credit notes approved by the sales team that raised them.

evidence.title: Industry cases
evidence.body: Most losses in similar firms come from supplier bank-detail fraud (fake emails changing payee details) and credit-note abuse.

options.label: Credit notes approved by the team that raised them
Payroll (with HR and finance checks in place)

questions.prompt: Which control do you implement first?

options.label: Call-back verification of every supplier bank-detail change, using contact details already on file
options.feedback: Cheap, fast, and stops the most common large fraud.

options.label: Fraud awareness e-learning
options.feedback: Useful, but weaker than a hard control on payments.

questions.prompt: Industry data: about 1 in 400 bank-detail change requests is fraudulent; Valtren gets about 600 a year; average fraudulent payment 45,000. Expected annual loss without verification?

options.label: 27 million
options.feedback: That multiplies every request by the loss.
One fraud; the expected number is 1.5.

questions.prompt: How should fraud risk be governed?

options.label: A named fraud risk owner in Finance, the assessment refreshed annually, and incidents and control testing reported to the Audit Committee
The risk team owns fraud
options.feedback: Second line advises; Finance owns the controls.

lesson: Fraud risk concentrates where money moves with weak verification. Fix the highest-loss control first, quantify it, and give fraud an owner.
